title: An astrophysical robbery
caption: The jellyfish galaxy NGC 3312 in the Hydra I cluster, imaged by ESO

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Right at the center of this frame, the spiral galaxy NGC 3312 looks almost smeared across the view, as if spilling its contents into the space around it. The frame shows a small part of the Hydra I cluster, which holds hundreds of galaxies, and NGC 3312 is the largest spiral galaxy known in that cluster.

The smudged look comes from a process called ram pressure stripping. A galaxy moving through a dense fluid, such as the hot gas that fills the space between galaxies in a cluster, feels that gas dragging on the colder gas in its outer layers. The drag pulls the cold gas away and lets it leak out.

Cold gas is what stars form from, so a galaxy that loses it this way risks a shrinking population of stars. Affected galaxies, usually ones falling toward the center of a cluster, tend to end up with long tendrils of gas trailing behind them. That appearance gives them the nickname jellyfish galaxies.

understand.summary: ESO does not name the telescope, instrument or filters used for this picture, and the color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The galaxy and its stripped gas are far too faint to see with the eye, and a telescope exposure gathers much more light.

explore: The picture was released as an ESO Picture of the Week and is credited to ESO, INAF, M. Spavone and E. Iodice. Besides NGC 3312, the frame holds hundreds of other small blips, and each galaxy in the cluster has its own history.
